case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Tyner v. Department of Social & Health Services, Child Protective Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that RCW 26.44.050 impliedly creates a negligent-investigation cause of action in favor of a child's parents, including parents themselves suspected of abuse, and that a later judicial no-contact order does not automatically break legal causation unless all material information was placed before the court.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the governing duty standard once a report is accepted: the agency must act reasonably, not flawlessly, toward both child and parents.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that under RCW 26.44.050, CPS owes a duty of care to a child's parents, even those suspected of abusing their own children, when investigating allegations of child abuse.

key_cases.case_name: M.W. v. Department of Social & Health Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that the implied negligent-investigation action under RCW 26.44.050 is a narrow exception limited to biased or faulty investigations producing a harmful placement decision, and does not reach other investigative harms such as an intrusive physical examination of the child.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the narrow-exception framework governing the quality of an accepted investigation.
key_cases.quote: such a claim is available only when DSHS conducts a biased or faulty investigation that leads to a harmful placement decision

key_cases.holding: The court held that the statutory duty to investigate is triggered only by a report of abuse or neglect that has already occurred, so a parent's prediction of future harm from a proposed placement did not invoke DSHS's duty under former RCW 26.44.050.
key_cases.relevance: Explains which communications the agency must accept for investigation and which it may decline.
key_cases.quote: Generally, a report initiates the dependency process. The duty to investigate cannot be invoked until receipt of a report.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc in a case arising from the Wenatchee, Washington child sex abuse investigations, the court held there is no constitutional right to have child witnesses interviewed in a particular manner, and that a deliberate-fabrication claim requires evidence that investigators knew or should have known the accused was innocent or used techniques so coercive they knew would yield false information.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the constitutional floor, and the wide latitude, governing how investigators may question child witnesses.
key_cases.quote: an allegation that an interviewer disbelieved an initial denial and continued with aggressive questioning of the child cannot, without more, support a deliberate-fabrication-of-evidence claim

key_cases.holding: The court held that the implied negligent-investigation action under chapter 26.44 RCW reaches only an investigation that leads to a harmful placement decision by the State, and refused to extend it to a 'constructive placement' where the parents themselves sent the child out of the home, affirming dismissal of a jury award arising from the Wenatchee investigations.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that the quality of an accepted investigation is actionable only through the placement decision it produces, not through the investigation's other consequences.
key_cases.quote: We decline Petitioners' request to enlarge the negligent investigation cause of action under chapter 26.44 RCW to include speculative harms argued as "constructive placement."

key_cases.case_name: Yonker v. Department of Social & Health Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that the public duty doctrine does not shield DSHS from a negligence claim by a mother and child whose reports of possible abuse the Department declined to investigate, because they fall within the particular and circumscribed class chapter 26.44 RCW was enacted to protect, and reversed summary judgment for the State.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that the duty to accept and investigate is judicially enforceable and is not defeated by the public duty doctrine.
key_cases.quote: If there is a question whether a report is sufficient to invoke the duty to investigate, that issue will be resolved on a case-by-case basis.
